findings.claim: The design misstates what list_threads returns, so the All tab cannot meet its requirement without changing v1 behavior.
findings.evidence: design.md:27 says the existing list_threads query 'returns open and resolved rows' and design.md:28 says All calls it 'unchanged'. thread_store.py:26 filters "AND status = 'open'". design.md:11 requires All to show open and resolved threads; design.md:12 and :29 require v1 to keep its current behavior through the same function.
findings.rationale: If the function stays unchanged, All shows only open threads, which violates design.md:11. If it is changed to return resolved rows, v1 clients begin receiving resolved threads, which violates design.md:12. The plan needs a separate query or parameter for v2.

findings.claim: Thread detail reads skip the document membership check, so non-members can read private thread content.
findings.evidence: design.md:23 says the detail route's dependencies are only require_session and load_thread. design.md:25 applies require_document_read only to mutations. design.md:13 requires current membership for every read. design.md:7 says bodies contain private document excerpts. design.md:24 says thread IDs are stored in shareable sidebar URLs. design.md:56 says load_thread looks a thread up by primary key only.
findings.rationale: Any authenticated user who gets a thread URL, including a former member whose membership was revoked, receives the thread and replies with private excerpts. A UUIDv4 ID cannot be guessed, but these IDs are shared on purpose, so it does not control access.

findings.claim: The writer pool's maximum capacity is below the required reply throughput.
findings.evidence: design.md:14 requires 600 reply creates/s sustained for 30 minutes, each stored within 1 s. design.md:36 sends all reply creates through the writer pool. design.md:37 caps each worker at 75 commits/s, and design.md:38 allows at most 6 workers. 6 x 75 = 450/s.
findings.rationale: At 600/s the queue grows by at least 150 commands per second, so commit latency rises without bound and exceeds 1 s almost immediately. The 600/s load test that gates promotion (design.md:68) cannot pass as designed.

findings.claim: v2 list responses promise reply_count, but the function they call unchanged does not select it.
findings.evidence: design.md:30 says v2 list responses add reply_count. design.md:28 says the All tab calls list_threads unchanged. thread_store.py:25 selects only id, document_id, body, status and created_at.
findings.rationale: As written, the v2 list cannot fill in reply_count. Either the function changes, which conflicts with design.md:28-29, or an extra per-list query is needed that the design does not describe.

findings.claim: Keyset pagination conflicts with reusing list_threads unchanged and filtering its result for the Open tab.
findings.evidence: design.md:31 specifies keyset pagination on (created_at, id) at 50 per page. thread_store.py:20-22 has no cursor or limit parameters and fetchall() returns every matching row. design.md:28 filters Open by status after the call.
findings.rationale: Each page request loads the document's full thread set and then cuts it in the application. That is not keyset pagination at the query level, and the per-request cost grows with the number of threads.

uncertainties: design.md:25 and :35 do not say whether membership is checked at enqueue time or rechecked inside the writer transaction. A reply from a user whose membership is revoked while the command is queued could still commit.
design.md:40 returns the stored reply when a request_id is retried, but does not say what happens if the retry has a different body.
design.md:56-58: load_thread returns 404 before the membership check returns 403, so a non-member can tell whether a thread ID exists. Whether that matters is not covered by the sources.
design.md:58 says 403 matches 'the existing source', but thread_store.py:4-17 only raises Forbidden. The HTTP mapping is not in the supplied code.
design.md:64 and :71: adding reply_count with a constant DEFAULT avoids rewriting rows only on PostgreSQL 11 or later. The server version is not stated.
design.md:70: after rollback, v1 (thread_store.py:26) hides threads resolved through v2 and has no way to reopen them. It is unclear whether that is acceptable.
design.md:45 clears the reply body on deletion, but the replies.body column at design.md:53 has no stated nullability or tombstone value.
design.md:68 lists membership, retry and load tests as promotion gates. None has been shown to pass.

findings.claim: The design says member_balances already exists and that append_entry upserts it in the same transaction as each entry. The current code does not do this, so redemption step 3 reads a balance that nothing maintains.
findings.evidence: design.md:71-73 says "The table already exists: `append_entry` upserts it in the same transaction as each entry insert, as ADR-001 requires." In src/ledger.py:17-26, append_entry only INSERTs into ledger_entries. get_balance (ledger.py:29-35) computes SUM(delta) over ledger_entries and never touches member_balances. design.md:81 also says "No other schema changes".
findings.rationale: If the table is missing, step 3 fails and every redemption errors. If the table exists but is not updated, the 409 check at design.md:64 compares against a stale value. That can approve redemptions that take the real balance below zero, breaking R3 (design.md:20), or wrongly reject valid ones. The cache-consistency rule in ADR-001:12-13 is assumed to hold but is not implemented.

findings.claim: Earn deduplication relies only on a Redis key with a 24-hour TTL, but the bus can replay up to 7 days back. Replayed order.paid events credit points again, which breaks R2.
findings.evidence: design.md:13-14: the bus "replays a topic from any offset within the last 7 days". design.md:44-45: the key is set "with a 24-hour TTL" only after the ledger write commits. earn_for_order (ledger.py:38-45) appends an earn with source_ref order:<order_id> and never checks for an existing one. ix_ledger_source_ref (design.md:80-81) is not declared unique. Unlike redeem_reversal (design.md:38, 69), the earn path has no 'unless one already exists' rule.
findings.rationale: A replay of events older than 24 hours produces a second earn entry, and also a second clawback, for the same order. Duplicates also occur without a long replay: (a) a worker crashes after the DB commit but before the Redis SET, so the event is redelivered; (b) two workers receive the same delivery at once and both find the key absent. R2 (design.md:19) requires exactly-once crediting "including across replays". These duplicates also break finance reconciliation, which the design's done criteria rely on (design.md:109-110).

findings.claim: The ledger service never checks that the member_id in the request matches the authenticated session. Any logged-in member can redeem or view another member's points.
findings.evidence: design.md:53-56: the body carries {member_id, order_id, points}. The gateway checks only the JWT "signature and expiry", and the ledger service "accepts gateway-authenticated requests as is". GET /v1/members/{member_id}/balance (design.md:93) and the cancel endpoint (design.md:92) take caller-supplied identifiers with no ownership check.
findings.rationale: R5 (design.md:22) says members can view and redeem only their own points. With the described flow, a valid token for member A plus member_id=B in the body debits B's balance. Changing the path parameter likewise exposes B's balance.

uncertainties: Capacity headroom: R6 means 600 order events/s and 150 redemptions/s (design.md:23). The consumer is quoted at 640 events/s (design.md:47-49), about 94% utilisation. Losing one of the 4 workers leaves 480/s, and R1's 2-minute p99 at peak is not shown. The redemption tier is 6 x 25 = 150 req/s (design.md:75), with zero headroom. It is not stated whether 25 req/s per pod already meets R4's 150 ms p99. The load-test figures are claims, not verified results.

Cancel before redeem: the cancel endpoint (design.md:67-69) appends "that redeem_reversal entry" but does not say what happens when no redeem:<order_id> entry exists, or what amount it uses. A redeem that arrives late or is retried after the cancel may still debit points for an order that was never placed.

Refund handling: order.refunded carries no amount (design.md:86), so partial refunds are undefined. It is also unclear whether events for one order arrive in order. If a refund is processed before its order.paid, the clawback finds no earn, and the later earn leaves the member credited.

Rollback (design.md:106-107) assumes unacked events survive a pause. That holds only if the pause is shorter than bus retention (7-day replay window, design.md:14). After step 3 deletes the batch (design.md:102), there is no fallback earn path.

During rollout the nightly batch also calls earn_for_order (design.md:8-9, 99-101), which takes no advisory lock and has no DB-level dedupe. Correctness at cutoff T depends on occurred_at filtering alone.

The Entry.kind comment (src/ledger.py:12) omits redeem_reversal, which design.md:80 adds. It is unknown whether a DB constraint on kind exists that would reject the new kind, despite "No other schema changes" (design.md:81).

Redemption step 2 (design.md:62) looks up redeem:<order_id> without scoping it to member_id or checking that points match. A retry with different points silently returns the original entry. Whether that is intended is not stated.

The per-member advisory lock (design.md:40-41, 61) is planned work and does not exist in src/ledger.py yet. append_entry opens its own transaction block (ledger.py:18), so the lock and the insert share one transaction only if the caller wraps both in an outer transaction.

findings.claim: The redemption balance check reads a member_balances cache that the current code does not maintain, and the design adds no schema or code change to create it.
findings.evidence: design.md:71-73 says the table already exists and that append_entry upserts it in the same transaction. src/ledger.py:17-26 shows append_entry only inserts into ledger_entries, and src/ledger.py:29-35 computes the balance as SUM(delta) over ledger_entries. design.md:81 says 'No other schema changes'.
findings.rationale: Step 3 (design.md:63) would read a missing or stale row. That either makes redemption fail or lets the 409 check pass against a wrong balance, which breaks R3 (design.md:20). ADR-001 (adr-001:12-13) allows a stored balance only as a cache written in the same transaction as each entry. That would need an append_entry change plus a backfill, and the design includes neither.

findings.claim: Earn and clawback processing is not idempotent across bus replays or crash/redelivery, so R2 does not hold.
findings.evidence: design.md:13-14: the bus replays from any offset within the last 7 days. design.md:43-45: the dedupe key evt:<event_id> has a 24-hour TTL and is set only after the ledger commit. earn_for_order (src/ledger.py:38-45) appends without checking for an existing order:<order_id> entry. ix_ledger_source_ref (design.md:80-81) is not declared unique. The clawback path (design.md:35-36) has no 'unless one already exists' guard, unlike redeem_reversal (design.md:37-38).
findings.rationale: Replaying events older than 24 hours, or a crash between the commit and the Redis SET, re-runs the write. That credits a paid order twice, which breaks R2 (design.md:19), or applies a refund clawback twice. Under ADR-002 (adr-002:11-13) a clawback is applied in full even below zero, so a duplicate clawback takes points the member legitimately holds.

findings.claim: No component checks that the authenticated member owns the member_id being redeemed or viewed, so R5 does not hold.
findings.evidence: design.md:54-56: the gateway validates only the JWT signature and expiry, and the ledger service accepts gateway-authenticated requests as is. member_id comes from the request body (design.md:54) or the URL path (design.md:93). No step compares it with the token's subject. The cancel endpoint (design.md:67-69) has no ownership check either.
findings.rationale: Any member with a valid session can redeem another member's points against their own order_id, read anyone's balance, or cancel another member's redemption. This directly breaks R5 (design.md:22).

uncertainties: Redemption capacity is exactly at the stated peak with no headroom: 6 pods x 25 req/s = 150 req/s = 9,000/min (design.md:75 vs design.md:23). Losing one pod or doing a rolling deploy at peak would drop below R6, and R4 latency at full saturation is unverified.

Earn capacity of 640 events/s (design.md:47-49) leaves about 40 events/s above the 600 events/s peak (design.md:23). Draining a multi-day replay or a paused backlog (design.md:106-107) while live traffic continues could exceed R1's 2-minute bound. The 160 events/s figure is a load-test result, not production evidence, and the topic's partition count, which limits parallelism to 4 workers, is not stated.

The cancel endpoint (design.md:67-69) does not say what happens when no redeem:<order_id> entry exists, or when cancel arrives before a timed-out redemption retry commits. In the second case the redemption could succeed after the cancel, leaving points spent on an order that was never placed.

When a redemption is retried with the same order_id but a different points value, or after it was cancelled, step 2 (design.md:62) returns 200 with the original entry. Whether that response is intended is not specified.
order.refunded carries no amount (design.md:86), so only full refunds can be represented. Whether partial refunds occur is not covered by the sources.

The kind comment at src/ledger.py:12 omits redeem_reversal, which design.md:80 lists. If the database restricts kind values, this would be a real schema change, which would contradict 'No other schema changes' (design.md:81). The workspace does not show which.

Rollback relies on unacked events staying on the bus (design.md:106-107). A pause longer than the 7-day replay window (design.md:13-14) could lose events, and once the batch is deleted (design.md:102) there is no fallback earn path.
Who handles refund clawbacks for the cohort before the cutover (design.md:99-101) is not stated. The context (design.md:8-9) describes the batch as calling only earn_for_order.

findings.claim: The redemption balance check depends on a member_balances cache that the current code does not maintain, and the design plans no work to add it.
findings.evidence: design.md:71-73 says member_balances 'already exists' and that append_entry 'upserts it in the same transaction as each entry insert'. src/ledger.py:17-26 shows append_entry only INSERTs into ledger_entries. src/ledger.py:29-35 computes balance by SUM over ledger_entries. design.md:81 says 'No other schema changes'.

With a stale or high balance, step 4 lets a redemption take the true balance below zero, which breaks R3 (design.md:20). With a low one, valid redemptions get a 409. findings.claim: Earn and clawback deduplication cannot meet R2 ('exactly once, including across replays').
findings.evidence: design.md:13-14: the bus replays from any offset within the last 7 days. design.md:45: Redis dedupe keys have a 24-hour TTL and are set only after the ledger commit. earn_for_order (ledger.py:38-45) appends with no check for an existing source_ref 'order:<id>'. ix_ledger_source_ref (design.md:80-81) is a plain index, not a unique one. findings.rationale: If a replay is more than 24 hours old, the keys have expired and every order.paid is credited again. A crash or redelivery between the commit and the Redis SET, or two workers picking up the same redelivered event, also writes duplicates. Replayed refunds append duplicate clawbacks, and ADR-002 lets those push balances further negative. Under ADR-001:10-11 the extra rows can only be fixed with compensating entries, and they distort the reconciliation at design.md:109-110.

findings.claim: Nothing ties the request's member_id to the authenticated member, so R5 is not enforced.
findings.evidence: design.md:54-56: the gateway checks only the JWT signature and expiry, and the ledger service 'accepts gateway-authenticated requests as is'. member_id comes from the request body (design.md:54) or the path (design.md:93). The cancel endpoint (design.md:68-69, 92) is keyed only by order_id.
findings.rationale: Any member with a valid session can redeem another member's points by sending that member's member_id, read any member's balance, and cancel redemptions by order_id. This directly breaks R5 (design.md:22), 'view and redeem only their own points'.

findings.claim: The code's documented entry kinds do not include the new redeem_reversal kind.
findings.evidence: ledger.py:12 lists kinds 'earn, redeem, clawback'. design.md:80 adds 'redeem_reversal', and design.md:81 says there are no other schema changes.
findings.rationale: The design adds a kind that the code's model does not declare. Any validation or constraint built from the existing list would reject reversal entries, so cancels and refunds would fail to return points.

uncertainties: Redemption capacity is 6 pods x 25 req/s = 150 req/s, which equals the R6 peak of 9,000/min (design.md:23, 75) with no headroom. Whether p99 stays under 150 ms (R4) at full utilization, or with a pod down during a deploy, is unverified.

Earn capacity is 4 x 160 = 640 events/s against a 600 events/s peak (design.md:23, 47-49), about 7% headroom. The load test may predate the member_balances upsert and the Redis round trips, so throughput with those included is unknown.

The design does not say how orders.v2 is partitioned. If order.refunded can be handled before order.paid for the same order, the clawback of 'points the order earned' (design.md:35) may be zero while the earn still lands later.

If a redemption for the same order_id is retried after a cancel, step 2 (design.md:62) returns the existing redeem entry with 200, even though it has been reversed. The design does not say whether order_ids can be reused this way.
The design does not define what cancel (design.md:67-69) does when no redeem entry exists for the order_id.

findings.claim: The aggregator double-counts clicks that are delivered more than once, so invoiced counts in daily_clicks are not exact.
findings.evidence: ADR-001 (docs/adr-001-click-event-bus.md:11-13) says delivery is at-least-once: an event may arrive again after a producer retry or a consumer restart, and each event carries an event_id. design.md:31-35 inserts each batch and adds its per-(code, day) counts to daily_clicks, then commits the offset after the transaction. design.md:54 and :58 define no uniqueness on event_id and no dedup step.
findings.rationale: If a worker crashes after the DB commit but before the offset commit, the whole batch is replayed and its counts are added to daily_clicks a second time. A producer retry also creates a duplicate event with the same event_id, and that duplicate gets counted too. Committing the offset after the transaction prevents lost clicks but causes duplicates. This breaks R3 (design.md:18), and paid workspaces are overbilled (README.md:4-5).

findings.claim: The pipeline's capacity is below the stated campaign peak, so analytics lag goes far past 60 s during a campaign.
findings.evidence: R2 (design.md:16-17) requires 12,000 clicks/s sustained for up to 1 hour with lag under 60 s. The design gives 4 workers x 2,000 events/s = 8,000 events/s and compares this only with the 2,300/s average (design.md:38-39).
findings.rationale: At 12,000/s the backlog grows by 4,000 events/s, about 14.4 M events after one hour. Lag (backlog divided by 8,000/s) passes 60 s about 2 minutes into the peak and reaches about 30 minutes by the end of the hour. Clearing the backlog at the off-peak surplus of about 5,700/s takes roughly another 40 minutes. R2 is not met.

findings.claim: The new stats endpoint does no authorization, so any requester can read any link's stats.
findings.evidence: design.md:61-62: the endpoint "skips the session lookup; the code in the path identifies the link, so the CDN caches responses for 60 s." R4 (design.md:19) requires stats to be visible only to the owner. The current link_stats checks owner_id against user_id and returns 404 otherwise (src/redirect.py:32-37).
findings.rationale: Short codes are public because they appear in every shared short URL. Anyone who knows a code can fetch its daily totals and top referrers and countries, and the CDN serves the cached response to anyone for 60 s. This reverses the owner check that exists today and violates R4.

uncertainties: Storage headroom: the 9.6 TB figure (design.md:41-43) assumes exactly 400 days at the 2,300/s average. A monthly partition is dropped only once its newest row is older than 400 days (design.md:55-56), so up to about 430 days are kept (about 10.3 TB of 12 TB). Campaign peaks, other data on the analytics cluster and growth are not counted. This is not a defect on the stated numbers, but the margin is thin.

Redirect latency and availability now depend on the shared bus. ADR-001:10-12 has each redirect wait for an acks=all acknowledgement and retry until it gets one. Whether p99 under 50 ms (R1) holds is not shown. While the bus is unavailable, redirects stall instead of failing over, and the design does not say what happens then.

Adding dedup on event_id may lower the measured 2,000 events/s per worker (design.md:37-38). Also, if event_id uniqueness is enforced with a constraint on the month-partitioned click_events table, the partition key may have to be included, depending on the engine.

Rollout step 4 (design.md:73) removes record_click and the flag on a fixed one-week schedule. The done criterion (design.md:75-76) is not a gate for it, so the rollback path (design.md:78-79) could be removed before 7 good consecutive days have been seen.
Late or replayed events update daily_clicks for past days. The sources do not say when invoices are cut from daily_clicks, so it is unclear whether corrections made after invoicing are reflected.

Four workers may update the same hot (code, day) row in concurrent transactions. Contention is lower than today, but lock ordering across multi-row batch updates is not specified, so deadlocks or retries are possible under campaign load.
During rollout, codes with the flag off have no click_events rows, so their referrer and country breakdowns will be empty or partial. The sources set no requirement for this period.

The 5-minute lookup cache (design.md:28-29) uses the whole deletion window in ADR-002:11-12. It complies as long as nothing else adds delay; negative caching and how the cache is invalidated on delete are not described.

findings.claim: The aggregator double-counts redelivered events, so daily_clicks is not exact and paid workspaces are overbilled.
findings.evidence: ADR-001 (docs/adr-001-click-event-bus.md:11-13) says delivery is at-least-once: an event can arrive again after a producer retry or a consumer restart. design.md:32-34 inserts every batch event into click_events and adds the batch counts to daily_clicks. Neither the aggregator nor click_events (design.md:54-56) checks or enforces uniqueness on event_id. R3 (design.md:18) requires exact counts, and README.md:4-5 says invoices are per tracked click.
findings.rationale: Suppose a worker commits its transaction and then crashes before committing the offset (design.md:34-35). The whole batch of up to 500 events is redelivered and counted again. A producer retry likewise leads to a second insert and a second increment. The design prevents lost clicks but does nothing about duplicates, so customers are invoiced for clicks that never happened.

findings.claim: Pipeline capacity is below the required campaign peak, so analytics lag misses R2 by a wide margin.
findings.evidence: R2 (design.md:16-17) requires sustaining 12,000 clicks/s for up to 1 hour with lag under 60 s. The pipeline is sized at 4 workers x 2,000 events/s = 8,000 events/s (design.md:37-38), and that figure is only compared with the 2,300 clicks/s average (design.md:39).
findings.rationale: At peak the backlog grows by 4,000 events/s. After an hour that is 14.4 M events, roughly 30 min of lag at 8,000/s. Once traffic falls back to the average, the 5,700/s of spare capacity needs about 42 more minutes to drain it. Meeting R2 would take at least 6 workers and partitions with no headroom, and more in practice.

findings.claim: The stats endpoint lets anyone who knows a link's code read that link's stats, which violates R4.
findings.evidence: design.md:61-62 says the endpoint skips the session lookup, treats the code in the path as identifying the link, and lets the CDN cache responses for 60 s. R4 (design.md:19) makes stats visible only to the link's owner. Today link_stats checks owner_id against user_id and returns 404 otherwise (src/redirect.py:32-37).
findings.rationale: Short codes are public because they are embedded in every shared URL. Without the session check, any visitor can read daily totals, referrers and countries. Path-keyed CDN caching would also serve those responses to anyone. This drops an access control that exists today.

uncertainties: R1 latency is not demonstrated. ADR-001:10-12 has the redirect wait for an acks=all acknowledgement and retry until acknowledged. The design gives no publish-latency figure that would support p99 under 50 ms at 12,000/s. It also doesn't say what redirects do during an event-bus outage, where unbounded retries would stall them.
Deduplicating on event_id inside click_events may require the unique key to include the partition column ts, depending on the database. Whether producer retries keep the same ts is not specified.

The topic is keyed by event_id (design.md:50), so a hot code's events spread across all 4 partitions and every worker updates the same daily_clicks (code, day) row. Whether this brings back contention or deadlocks depends on update ordering and on whether the 2,000 events/s load test (design.md:37-38) used a skewed, campaign-like code distribution. The design states neither.

Storage headroom is thin and based on averages. Monthly partitions are dropped only once their newest row is over 400 days old (design.md:55-56), so up to about 431 days are kept, roughly 10.3 TB of 12 TB (design.md:41-43). Campaign peaks and growth are not included.

With the backlog lag described in the findings, events can be added to a day's daily_clicks well after that UTC day ends. The design does not say when invoices read daily_clicks or how late increments are handled.

Rollout step 4 (design.md:73) removes record_click and the rollback flag one week after reaching 100%. That step is not tied to the 7-day done criterion (design.md:75-76), so the rollback path could disappear before the criterion is met.

A 5-minute lookup cache (design.md:28-29) matches the ADR-002 maximum (adr-002-immutable-links.md:11-12, 16). Any replica lag or negative caching would push deletion beyond the 5-minute window in the terms of service. Neither is specified.

findings.claim: The aggregator double-counts duplicate events in daily_clicks, so the exact invoiced counts required by R3 are not met.
findings.evidence: ADR-001 (docs/adr-001-click-event-bus.md:11-13) makes delivery at-least-once: an event can arrive more than once after a producer retry or a consumer restart, and it carries an event_id. design.md:32-34 inserts each batch into click_events and adds its per-(code, day) counts to daily_clicks, with no deduplication. design.md:34-35 commits the offset only after the transaction commits. design.md:54 gives click_events no uniqueness on event_id. R3 (design.md:18) requires exact counts because they are invoiced (README.md:4-5, design.md:10-11).
findings.rationale: If a worker crashes between the DB commit and the offset commit, it replays the whole batch, up to 500 events, and adds them to daily_clicks a second time. A producer retry can also put a second copy of an event on the topic. Either way the event is counted twice and paid workspaces are over-invoiced. Committing the offset after the transaction stops lost clicks but makes duplicates certain. Counts need to come only from event_ids that are new, inside the same transaction.

findings.claim: The pipeline can process 8,000 events/s, which is below the required 12,000 clicks/s campaign peak, so analytics lag goes far past 60 s.
findings.evidence: R2 (design.md:16-17) requires 12,000 clicks/s for up to 1 hour with lag under 60 s, and R1 (design.md:15) uses the same 12,000/s peak. design.md:37-39 gives 4 partitions x 2,000 events/s = 8,000 events/s and checks that only against the 2,300 clicks/s average.
findings.rationale: At peak the backlog grows by 4,000 events/s. Lag passes 60 s after about 2 minutes. After the 1-hour peak the backlog is about 14.4 M events, roughly 30 minutes of lag at 8,000/s, and it then drains at only 5,700/s above the average rate. With one worker per partition, throughput cannot grow without repartitioning the topic. Meeting the peak needs at least 6 partitions and workers at the measured rate, with no headroom.

findings.claim: The stats endpoint drops the owner check and is cached by the CDN per code, so anyone can see any link's stats, which violates R4.
findings.evidence: R4 (design.md:19) says a link's stats are visible only to its owner. design.md:61-62 says the endpoint skips the session lookup and the CDN caches responses for 60 s by code. The current link_stats (src/redirect.py:32-37) returns 404 unless owner_id matches user_id.
findings.rationale: Short codes are public because they appear in every shared URL. Anyone who knows a code gets daily totals, top referrers and top countries, and the shared CDN cache serves those responses to anyone for 60 s. This removes an access control that exists today. Owner authorization needs to stay, and the cache must be private or keyed per user.

uncertainties: ADR-001 (docs/adr-001-click-event-bus.md:10-11) requires an acks=all acknowledgement, retried until it succeeds, before each redirect is answered. design.md:26-27 follows this, but nothing shows that publish latency fits the 50 ms p99 of R1. During a bus outage, redirects would block or fail rather than degrade.

The storage estimate (design.md:41-43) uses the average rate. Under the monthly drop rule (design.md:55-56) a partition is dropped only once its newest row is past 400 days, so data is kept up to about 430 days: roughly 10.3 TB of the 12 TB. Campaign peaks, daily_clicks, and whether other data shares the cluster could shrink or remove that margin.

Stats are read from a replica (design.md:45-46), and responses are cached for 60 s (design.md:62). Neither replica lag nor cache age is counted in the 60 s lag budget of R2, so visible staleness can exceed 60 s even when aggregator lag is within it.

The day used for daily_clicks is not defined. Today it is wall-clock UTC at write time (src/redirect.py:15). The aggregator presumably uses the event ts. Late or replayed events near midnight would then land on a different day than they would under record_click. This matters only if invoices are cut per day before the backlog has drained.

A hot code's events spread across all 4 partitions because the key is event_id (design.md:50). All 4 workers then upsert the same (code, day) row concurrently. Contention per batch is much lower than per click, but lock waits or deadlocks between multi-row upserts are not addressed.

Step 4 removes record_click and the flag 'one week after reaching 100%' (design.md:73). The done criterion is 7 consecutive good days (design.md:75-76). The rollback path (design.md:78-79) could be removed before that criterion is actually met.
The design does not set topic retention. It must cover the worst-case backlog and any rollback drain so that no unconsumed events are lost.

The 5-minute lookup cache (design.md:28-29) sits exactly at the deletion window of ADR-002 (docs/adr-002-immutable-links.md:11-12, 16). That is compliant only if the cache is filled straight from the primary with no added propagation delay.
